translations.text: Evil, then, is the cessation of the activity of the powers lying within nature, the activity directed toward their end, and nothing else whatsoever.
Or again, it is the erring judgment of the natural powers, moved brutishly by something else, apart from their end.
And by "end" I mean the cause of beings, which all things naturally desire.
Even though the evil one, concealing his envy by pretense, toward something else among beings, apart from their cause,
rather changed by guile the desire and movement of man, and from this he begot ignorance of the cause.
Now then, evil is, as I said before, ignorance of that good cause of beings,
within which man, having come to be and having opened his senses wide, was wholly deprived of divine knowledge,
but filled with a passive knowledge of sensible things, which man received only through the senses, like grazing cattle.
And he found by experience that the reception of sensible things confirmed his visible bodily nature, and rightly, as a perceptible good;
that is, bereft of divine beauty, because of the visible creation he became ignorant of God, and for the strengthening of the flesh, because of his need, he made it a god.
And since the flesh had, as its own peculiar property, a natural kinship with what was supposed to be a god,
by a just reasoning he loved it, and with all eagerness, by showing care and diligence only for the flesh alone, he became a servant
of the creature instead of the Creator. For no one can serve the creature in any other way,
unless he becomes wholly devoted to the care of the flesh, just as neither can anyone serve God unless he purifies his soul through the virtues.
But man, as one fulfilling the corruption-working service of the flesh and made self-loving by it, had pleasure and pain incessantly at work in him,
as he was forever eating from that tree of disobedience, mingled of good and evil together, which could be known by experience through the senses.
And if anyone says that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the visible creation, he does not stray from the truth, for by nature the reception of it produces pleasure and pain.
And again, since the creation of visible things also has spiritual principles, which nourish the mind, and also a natural power, which delights the senses,
but weaning [?] the mind, it was named the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which has knowledge of good when contemplated spiritually, but
knowledge of evil when received bodily, since it becomes a teacher of the passions to those who receive it bodily, as drawing forgetfulness of the divine upon them.
For this reason God commanded human beings to postpone for the time being the reception of it, so that first, as was more just,
man might come to know his cause by grace through participation, and through such participation might make firm, by impassibility and immutability, the immortality given to him by grace.
And as one become god, through deification he might contemplate impassibly, in freedom together with God, the creatures of God, and be exalted by the knowledge of them,
as God and not as man, possessing by grace and with wisdom the same knowledge of beings that God has, for the deification of the mind and the transformation of sense-perception.

Thus, then, has it been said here concerning the tree, in a way suited to all, by such figurative interpretation as is possible, while the more mystical and more exalted account is preserved for those who have been made initiates in mind, and is honored by us with silence.
